title: A Corner of His Own
story:
They walked past shelves that smelled of dried lavender and old parchment. They walked past desks where inkwells sat dry like tiny hollow stones. They walked past tall arched windows where the morning sun was just beginning to slice through the dust motes. Barnaby walked with a slow, deliberate stride, his leather shoes clicking softly against the marble floor, and James followed closely, keeping his eyes on the gentle sway of the old man’s coat.

At the far edge of the rotunda, hidden behind a heavy tapestry depicting an ancient forest, Barnaby unlocked a small iron door. Beyond it lay a narrow, winding spiral staircase that curved upward into the shadows of the library’s dome. James climbed eagerly, his small hands gripping the cool iron railing. With every turn, the grand hall below fell further away, until the rumbling echoes of the town outside became nothing more than a faint, rhythmic whisper.

At the top of the stairs, Barnaby pushed open a low wooden door to reveal a tiny, circular room nestled high under the eaves. It was a forgotten archivist's nook, dusty but warm, with wooden rafters that curved like the ribs of a great ship. In the center of the room sat a sturdy wooden crate, and in the corner, a soft pile of discarded bookbinder’s wool lay like a ready-made nest. A single, round window looked out over the sprawling, tiled rooftops of Oakhaven.

Barnaby set down a small, unlit brass lantern on the crate and gave James a warm, encouraging nod, patting his shoulder before turning to leave him to rest. Left alone in the quiet sanctuary, James climbed up to the round window and looked out. He felt a familiar flutter of nervousness in his chest, so he closed his eyes and practiced his ritual, counting three distinct sounds: the distant chime of a street clock, the gentle whistling of the wind through the roof tiles, and the steady, comforting beat of his own heart.

Opening his eyes, James carefully lined up his treasures on the wooden crate: his brass canister, his charcoal, his sea-glass, and his new magnifying lens. Through the green glass, the chimneys of Oakhaven glowed like emerald towers. He rested his chin on the windowsill, watching a solitary grey pigeon preen its feathers on the stone ledge just outside, perfectly content in his new corner of the world.
